extracted.intended_audience: researchers, comedy writers, and general public interested in the psychology of humour
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and empirical findings about what makes jokes funny (elements, cognitive correlates, length, cultural preferences) based on LaughLab's large-scale ratings and brain-scan results. Useful for evaluating or writing jokes for varied audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality / cross-demographic appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: This joke 'works across many different countries, appeals to men and women, and young and old alike.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer jokes that do not rely on narrow cultural references or age/gender-specific knowledge; the winning hunters joke is cited as an example of 'real universal appeal.' Use language and situations readily understood by broad demographics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core psychological functions that make jokes funny
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes 'sometimes make us feel superior to others, reduce the emotional impact of anxiety-provoking situations, or surprise us because of some kind of incongruity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design jokes to invoke one or more of these functions—feelings of superiority, anxiety-reduction, or an incongruous surprise—since combining them (as the winning joke did) increases funniness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise / incongruity (setup leads audience one way, punchline reframes)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Most jokes work because they surprise us – they set us thinking in one direction, and then we hear the punchline and realise that there is a completely different way of seeing the situation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the setup to create a strong, but plausible, expectation and craft the punchline to force a rapid re-interpretation. Example given: two fish in a tank -> 'Do you know how to drive this?' (army tank reinterpretation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive complexity must match audience's frontal-lobe abilities
rubrics_metrics.description: People who perform well on frontal-lobe-type estimation tasks tended to prefer relatively complex jokes, while those who did not tended to prefer more straightforward jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess intended audience's cognitive style: for audiences high in flexible/frontal-lobe processing, use multi-step or conceptually layered jokes; for broader or less analytically-inclined audiences, prefer simpler, more direct humor (e.g., puns, one-line gags). Examples: complex scientist/philosopher lion joke vs simple 'Fry-Day' pun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimal joke length (~103 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: According to LaughLab data, 'jokes containing one hundred and three words are the funniest.' The winning joke is 102 words — 'almost the perfect length for a joke!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing narrative jokes, target roughly 100–105 words for maximal rating in this dataset; balance necessary context with concision to keep setup and punchline tight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal choice: ducks are funniest
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Jokes mentioning ducks were seen as funnier than other jokes... if you are going to tell a joke involving an animal, make it a duck.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer ducks when using animals as comedic elements; LaughLab data found ducks produced higher funniness ratings than other animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty matters — avoid overused/commonly submitted jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: The most frequently submitted joke ('What's brown and sticky? A stick') was submitted over 300 times 'And no-one ever found it funny.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid clichés and over-familiar punchlines; repetition and overexposure reduce perceived funniness. Freshness/novelty helps ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural / national preferences for joke types
rubrics_metrics.description: Different countries showed distinct preferences: 'The Republic of Ireland, the UK, Australia and New Zealand expressed a strong preference for jokes involving word plays'; 'Americans and Canadians much preferred gags where there was a sense of superiority'; 'Many European countries, such as France, Denmark and Belgium, liked jokes that were somewhat surreal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor joke type to national/cultural audience: favor wordplay and puns for UK/Australia/NZ/Ireland audiences; superiority-based humor (making someone look stupid) for US/Canada; surreal and absurd humor for parts of Europe. Use local testing where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making light of anxiety-provoking topics can be effective (culture-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'These European countries also enjoyed jokes that involved making light of topics that often make us feel anxious, such as death, illness, and marriage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate for the culture/audience, using taboo or anxiety-laden themes (death, illness, marriage) can increase funniness by reducing emotional impact; exercise caution, as acceptability varies by audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad, non-preferential audiences tend to rate a wider spectrum funnier
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Germans did not express a strong preference for any type of joke - this may well explain why they came first in our league table of funniness – they do not have any strong preferences and so tend to find a wide spectrum of jokes funny.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If targeting an international/mixed audience, favor jokes with cross-style appeal rather than niche formats; audiences without strong style preferences may reward variety and novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neural basis: prefrontal cortex and flexible thinking needed for understanding punchlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Brain scans showed a 'very precise area of the brain' (mainly in the prefrontal cortex) is involved in understanding why a joke is funny; this region 'plays a vital role in the type of flexible thinking needed to understand a joke.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft jokes that leverage rapid re-interpretation and cognitive flexibility; more conceptually demanding jokes rely on prefrontal processing and may not land with audiences lacking that processing style.
